ai.definition: Neural Link is a neurotechnological approach aimed at establishing direct, bidirectional communication between the human brain and external devices or computer systems. This technology seeks to enhance human-computer interaction by bypassing traditional input methods such as keyboards or mice.
ai.howItWorks: High-density electrode arrays are placed directly on the surface of the brain or embedded within it. These electrodes capture neural signals, which are then processed using advanced signal processing techniques to translate these signals into digital commands that can control external devices or software applications.
ai.problemSolved: Traditional input methods for controlling computers and other devices are slow and imprecise compared to natural human thought processes. Neural Link aims to overcome this by providing a direct interface between the brain and technology, enabling faster and more intuitive interactions.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves creating high-density electrode arrays that can be safely implanted in or on the brain. These arrays must be biocompatible and capable of long-term stable operation without causing damage to surrounding tissue.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing and fabricating the microelectrode arrays, integrating them with signal processing hardware and software, and developing methods for safe implantation and removal by medical professionals.
ai.costDrivers: High material costs for specialized electrodes, complex fabrication processes, and the need for precise surgical techniques drive up initial development and manufacturing costs. Long-term maintenance and potential revisions also contribute to ongoing expenses.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is in an early conceptual stage with significant challenges remaining before widespread adoption becomes feasible.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks for such invasive medical devices are currently underdeveloped, posing both legal and ethical hurdles that need to be addressed before commercialization can occur.
ai.risks: Safety concerns related to long-term implantation, potential adverse reactions from the body's immune system, and the risk of device failure or malfunction are major risks associated with this technology.
ai.profitability: Given the current state of development and regulatory challenges, profitability is not yet a realistic consideration. However, if successful, it could open up new markets in healthcare and consumer electronics.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future advancements may include improvements in electrode design for better signal capture, more efficient signal processing algorithms, and safer implantation techniques that reduce patient risk.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking. Implantable devices are expected to operate on minimal power supplies once implanted.

glossary.def: Arrays of microelectrodes designed to capture neural signals from specific areas of the brain with high precision.
Materials that are safe for use in biological environments without causing adverse reactions or damage to living tissues.

subsystems.name: Electrode array
subsystems.role: the sensor that intercepts electrical activity from individual neurons or small groups.
parts: flexible polymer threads or thin films

subsystems.name: Implanted electronics
subsystems.role: amplifies, digitises and transmits neural signals from inside the body.

subsystems.name: Hermetic enclosure
subsystems.role: protects electronics from body fluids and keeps the device biocompatible for years.

subsystems.name: Signal processing and decoding
subsystems.role: turns raw voltage spikes into commands a computer can use.

subsystems.name: External interface
subsystems.role: connects the decoded intent to a computer, prosthetic or stimulator.
parts: feedback or stimulation hardware (for bidirectional links)

buildSteps.title: Design the electrode array
buildSteps.detail: Choose channel count, geometry and material (silicon, polymer, or carbon fibre) to match the brain region and minimise scarring.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the array
buildSteps.detail: Use photolithography, thin-film deposition and etching to pattern microscopic electrodes and traces on a wafer or flexible substrate.

buildSteps.title: Encapsulate and test
buildSteps.detail: Coat the array in biocompatible polymer or ceramic, then test electrical impedance and durability in saline.

buildSteps.title: Build the implanted electronics
buildSteps.detail: Assemble an ASIC that amplifies and digitises signals, plus a wireless power and data link, in a hermetic package.

buildSteps.title: Integrate the device
buildSteps.detail: Connect the electrode array to the electronics, seal all feedthroughs, and run accelerated ageing tests.

buildSteps.title: Implant surgically
buildSteps.detail: Either open the skull and insert electrodes with a robotic assist, or thread a stent-like array through blood vessels, depending on the design.

buildSteps.title: Capture and decode signals
buildSteps.detail: Record neural activity, filter noise, detect spikes, and train a decoder to map patterns to intended movements or speech.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate with the user
buildSteps.detail: The patient practices tasks while the decoder is fine-tuned; calibration may need repeating as the brain adapts or electrodes shift.

prerequisites.why: arrays with hundreds to thousands of channels exist in research, but long-term stability is limited.
used in cochlear implants and other medical devices, but scaling to high channel counts is hard.

prerequisites.tech: Real-time spike sorting and decoding algorithms
prerequisites.why: motor intent can be decoded in trials, but robust, calibration-free decoding for complex tasks is not solved.
electrodes and seals degrade over months to years, causing signal loss.
robotic insertion and endovascular approaches are in early clinical trials, not routine.

pathway.milestone: clinical trials let people with paralysis control cursors and robotic arms via implanted arrays
pathway.unlocks: proof that high-bandwidth neural signals can restore some communication and control.

pathway.milestone: fully wireless, higher-channel implants with multi-year lifetime
pathway.unlocks: everyday use without cables or frequent surgery, starting with severe disability.

pathway.milestone: bidirectional links that also stimulate neurons to provide touch or sight feedback
pathway.unlocks: more natural control of prosthetics and sensory restoration.

pathway.milestone: scaled manufacturing and regulatory approval for broader medical use
pathway.unlocks: treatment of conditions such as epilepsy, depression or stroke rehabilitation — with general consumer use still speculative.
